description: I’m Masooma, a backend and data engineer in Seattle. I was part of NASA L’SPACE NPWEE, working on autonomy and AI, where I gained hands-on experience in how to approach complex challenges, identify meaningful problems, develop and refine technical ideas, and learn how to understand what NASA is actually asking for, identify the requirements and evaluation criteria, and use those criteria to assess and strengthen a proposal.
summary:
Around Herat, Afghanistan, it does not rain from June to October, so farmland only has a summer growing season if someone brings water to it. Humanitarian survey teams assess farmland household by household, across more than 43,000 hectares; by the time a survey finishes, the season is over.

OFFBEAT reads ten NISAR L-band radar passes from June to October 2026 and asks three questions of every hectare: did its radar echo at least double, when did it peak, and did it follow the fields around it? Radar sees through clouds and dust, so the answer does not depend on clear skies.

Of 435 km² of farmland, 54 km² changed strongly and 8.8 km² moved out of step with their neighbours, giving 163 places ranked largest first and printable as field cards. A blind check against NASA Sentinel-2 imagery at twenty random hectares agrees 8 of 20: summer peaks hold up well (6 of 8), while four of seven “quiet” hectares were actually green, so the method misses real growth.

It does not say why a field differs. It says where to look first.
details:
What it does. OFFBEAT turns ten NISAR radar passes over Herat, Afghanistan, into one map where every square is a hectare. Teal moved with its neighbours; orange did not, and grey had no clear season. Click a hectare, and you see its ten measurements, a chart against the surrounding fields, and a verdict that separates what was measured from what is only a hypothesis. Type how many places your team can visit, and print them as field cards with coordinates.

How it works. Three rules. Did the echo at least double? When did it peak? And did it follow the fields within half a kilometre? A hectare with fewer than four changed neighbours is not judged at all, rather than guessed at.

Why it matters. Survey teams assess Herat’s farmland household by household across 43,529 hectares. By the time they finish, the season is over. OFFBEAT narrows it to 163 places, works through cloud and dust, and repeats every twelve days.

What makes it different. Each field is judged against its own neighbours, not an absolute threshold — so it is compared with its own valley and its own weather. And every field can be heard: its season plays as a rhythm that speeds up as the crop grows. A radar chart excludes anyone who cannot read one. A rhythm does not.

Built honestly. Move the threshold and watch our headline number change. On 900 hectares of bare ground, zero false alarms. A blind check against NASA Sentinel-2 at twenty random hectares agrees 8 of 20 summer peaks hold up best at 6 of 8, while four of seven “quiet” hectares were actually green. OFFBEAT misses real growth, and the page says so.

Tools. Python (numpy, scipy, h5py, pyproj, earthaccess) and Leaflet. Static files, no server, no login, fully open source.

It does not say why a field differs. It says where to look first.
